'Diabetes Mela' app to provide info on diabetes risk, diagnosis, treatment

15 November, 2026, 12:05 am
Last modified: 15 November, 2026, 12:21 am

Against the backdrop of increasing prevalence of diabetes across the country, an app titled 'Diabetes Mela' is being developed to provide information on diabetes risk assessment, disease management and healthy lifestyles. 

Details of the app were shared at a press conference organised at the conference room of the Dhaka Reporters' Unity (DRU) in the capital yesterday (14 November), marking World Diabetes Day.

At the press conference, Dr Selim unveiled the logo of the Diabetes Mela app.

He said the app would be developed and finalised based on feedback from the people it was intended to serve. He invited members of the public to submit their suggestions by 31 January 2027.

Feedback can be submitted through a designated form, the app's Facebook page, WhatsApp at 01701-665465 or by scanning a QR code.

People at risk will receive relevant information and guidance on healthy living, while those diagnosed with diabetes will have access to various forms of treatment-related support.

The app will help both patients and at-risk individuals become more aware of and responsible for managing their health, he added.

At the conference, Dr Md Fazle Rabbi Khan, chief coordinator of Diabetes Mela, said the app would help users gain an initial understanding of whether they are at risk of developing diabetes or already have the disease.

Dr Shahjada Selim, a member of the advisory council of Diabetes Mela, associate professor at BMU and elected president of the Bangladesh Endocrine Society, said diabetes had assumed epidemic proportions worldwide, with its prevalence rising at an alarming rate in Bangladesh.

One in every 10 people in the country has diabetes, yet 62.1% of those affected are unaware of their condition, he said. Unhealthy eating habits, lack of physical activity, obesity and inadequate awareness increase the risk of diabetes, he added.

Despite the rising prevalence of diabetes, 62% of people with the disease remain unaware that they have it. Moreover, most diagnosed patients fail to keep their blood sugar levels under control, increasing their risk of complications such as heart disease, stroke, kidney failure and vision loss.

Dr Selim further said blood sugar levels were uncontrolled in 92% of diabetes patients in Bangladesh.

This increases the risk of heart disease, stroke, kidney failure, vascular complications, and damage to the eyes and nerves. Such complications not only disrupt patients' normal lives but also increase treatment costs, placing additional pressure on families and the healthcare system, he said.

Separately, at a discussion organised by the Bangladesh Diabetic Samity at Birdem in Dhaka, former caretaker government adviser and executive chairman of the Power and Participation Research Centre Hossain Zillur Rahman highlighted the importance of developing private healthcare and voluntary service organisations alongside state initiatives.

Zillur said it was not possible to ensure all kinds of services for citizens by relying solely on the state. The development of private and voluntary service organisations outside the government framework was therefore equally important, he said.

He praised the Bangladesh Diabetic Samity for developing into a major service-oriented organisation and expanding its activities across different parts of the country, describing its experience as an example for developing nations.
